docs.title: RAS 304 — Individual Component Selection Report
docs.text: Name: Emmanuel Garcia Assigned Module: Board 2 – Grip Actuation Node Course: RAS 304 Embedded Systems Design

docs.title: Subsystem 1: Bidirectional H-Bridge Motor Driver
docs.text:
The H-bridge converts microcontroller control signals into power for the DC motor. It supports forward and reverse operation and PWM speed control for opening and closing the gripper.

Solution Pros Cons Option 1: Cytron MD13SEstimated cost: $15.30Product page • MOSFET-based switching.• Bidirectional motor control.• Simplifies wiring. • Higher cost than a basic driver IC.• Requires enclosure space.• Stall-current compatibility must be verified. Option 2: L298N H-BridgeEstimated cost: $3.15Product reference • Low cost.• Widely documented.• Supports two motor channels. • Significant voltage drop.• More heat.• Lower efficiency. Option 3: Discrete MOSFET H-BridgeEstimated cost: $4.20Circuit reference • Customizable design.• Potentially low conduction losses.• Flexible PCB layout. • More complex design.• Shoot-through risk.• More testing required.

docs.title: Final Selection: Cytron MD13S
docs.text: The Cytron MD13S is the preferred candidate because it integrates the power switching required for bidirectional DC motor control. The final motor variant must be checked against the driver's continuous and peak current ratings before implementation.

docs.title: Subsystem 2: Current Sensing and Overload Protection
docs.text:
This subsystem measures motor current using a shunt resistor and a signal-conditioning circuit. The microcontroller reads the current measurement and responds to an overload condition.

Solution Pros Cons Option 1: Texas Instruments TLV9002Estimated cost: $0.83Official datasheet • Dual operational amplifier.• Can amplify a shunt voltage.• Low component cost. • Requires external circuitry.• Not a dedicated comparator.• Input/output limits must be checked. Option 2: Analog Devices AD8210Estimated cost: $7.85Manufacturer reference • Dedicated current-sense amplifier.• Designed for shunt measurements.• Simplifies signal amplification. • Higher cost.• Requires a separate threshold detector.• Package availability must be verified. Option 3: Discrete BJT Threshold CircuitEstimated cost: $0.35Circuit reference • Low cost.• Basic components.• Simple threshold concept. • Temperature-sensitive threshold.• Lower measurement accuracy.• Requires careful tuning.

docs.title: Final Selection: Texas Instruments TLV9002
docs.text:
The TLV9002 is a candidate for the current-sensing circuit because its two amplifier channels can support signal amplification and threshold detection with appropriate external components. The circuit must be designed and tested for the selected motor's current range.

The TLV9002 is an operational amplifier, not a dedicated comparator. If fast fault detection is required, a dedicated comparator may be more suitable.

docs.title: Subsystem 3: DC Motor and Lead-Screw Assembly
docs.text:
This subsystem supplies the torque required to actuate the gripper fingers. The gearmotor drives a lead screw through a compatible shaft coupler, converting rotational motion into linear movement.

Solution Pros Cons Option 1: Pololu 25D Metal GearmotorEstimated cost: $19.95Product page • Metal gearbox.• Multiple gear ratios.• Standard 4 mm D-shaped shaft on applicable versions. • Requires lead screw and coupler.• Needs a mounting bracket.• Stall current depends on motor variant. Option 2: N20 Micro GearmotorEstimated cost: $9.50Product reference • Compact design.• Lightweight.• Low estimated cost. • May provide insufficient gripping torque.• Small gears may be less suitable for heavy loads.• Requires mechanical integration. Option 3: Micro Linear ActuatorEstimated cost: $55.00Manufacturer reference • Integrated linear drive.• Simplifies mechanical assembly.• Some models include limit switches. • Higher cost.• Fixed dimensions.• Specifications vary by model.

docs.title: Final Selection: Pololu 25D Metal Gearmotor
docs.text:
The Pololu 25D gearmotor is the preferred candidate because it offers multiple gear ratios and a durable gearbox. A compatible shaft coupler, lead screw, and mechanical supports will be required.

The motor's voltage, gear ratio, rated current, and stall current must be verified before purchase. The overload circuit should stop the motor when excessive current is detected. Limit switches or another suitable travel-limiting mechanism should prevent excessive movement.

docs.title: Microcontroller Pin Mapping
docs.text:
These are proposed assignments and must be verified against the exact microcontroller model.

Pin Connection Direction Signal Function RC0 H-Bridge Output PWM Motor speed control. RC1 H-Bridge Output GPIO Motor direction. RA1 Current-sense circuit Input ADC Measures motor current. RE1 Overload detector Input GPIO/interrupt Detects an overload alert. RD2 Board 1 hub Input UART RX Receives commands. RD3 Board 1 hub Output UART TX Sends status information. RB0 Board 1 hub Input GPIO Emergency-stop signal.

Verify the pin functions, voltage levels, and peripheral routing for the selected microcontroller before wiring.

docs.title: Part 2: Power Budget and Voltage Regulation
docs.text:
The regulator provides a stable 5 V logic supply. The motor must use a suitably rated motor power path.

Solution Pros Cons Option 1: L7805 / LM7805Estimated cost: $0.62Manufacturer reference • Simple three-terminal regulator.• Regulated 5 V output.• Thermal and short-circuit protection. • Converts excess voltage into heat.• Lower efficiency than switching regulators.• Requires thermal evaluation. Option 2: Murata OKI-78SR-5/1.5-W36-CEstimated cost: $4.85Manufacturer reference • Switching conversion is generally more efficient.• Reduces heat for large voltage drops.• Compact power-conversion solution. • Higher cost.• Switching ripple may affect analog measurements.• Requires suitable decoupling and layout.

docs.title: Final Selection: L7805 / LM7805
docs.text:
The L7805 is a candidate for the initial low-current logic rail because it is simple to integrate. Its thermal performance must be checked using the actual input voltage and load current.

For a 12 V input, 5 V output, and 50 mA load:

\[ P_{\text{loss}}=(12-5)(0.05)=0.35\text{ W} \]

The regulator dissipates approximately 0.35 W as heat under these assumptions. A heatsink requirement depends on the package and operating conditions.

A switching regulator should be reconsidered if battery runtime or heat becomes a major concern.

docs.title: Estimated Component Budget
docs.text:
Component Estimated Cost Cytron MD13S $15.30 TLV9002 $0.83 Pololu 25D gearmotor $19.95 L7805 / LM7805 $0.62 Estimated subtotal $36.70

The subtotal excludes the lead screw, shaft coupler, mounting hardware, limit switches, shunt resistor, passive components, wiring, and power supply. Prices must be confirmed before purchasing.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Board 2 controls the gripper actuator, monitors motor load, and communicates operating status to the bus master. The proposed components prioritize cost, integration, and flexibility during prototyping.

Before final implementation, the team must verify motor current requirements, driver compatibility, overload response, regulator thermal performance, and microcontroller pin assignments. The assembled lead-screw mechanism must also be tested to ensure that it produces the required gripping force and travel safely.

Image note: The images above are illustrative references and may not depict the exact model listed. Confirm all component specifications using the linked manufacturer documentation.

The final design should include a reliable method for stopping the motor during an overload, detecting excessive travel, and entering a safe state during an emergency stop.

Note: All listed prices are estimates for comparison. Final component selection must be based on verified datasheets, exact model numbers, and the electrical and mechanical requirements of the assembled gripper.
